title: Walking with modesty
hook: one of the two women comes to him walking with modesty (28:25)

segments.voice: Yesterday, farigh, and your line was a heart held steady. Did you send the short message to someone who's afraid? Day five hundred twenty-five, the end of the week.

Musa is a grown man now, and on the run. He has fled Egypt, alone, and walked all the way to Madyan. He arrives at a well where shepherds are crowding their flocks in to drink. Standing back, holding their animals away, are two women. He asks what's wrong. They say they can't water until the shepherds leave, and their father is a very old man. So Musa waters their flock for them. Then he goes and sits in the shade, exhausted, with nothing, and prays. And then someone comes walking toward him.
screen: `A MAN ON THE RUN, AT A WELL.`
`HE SITS IN THE SHADE AND PRAYS.`

segments.voice: His prayer in the shade is one line long. Pickthall: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." No plan, no demand. Just: I need whatever You send. And what's sent comes walking. Pickthall: "Then there came unto him one of the two women, walking shyly." The Arabic says she walked 'ala istihya', upon shyness, upon modesty. The classical dictionaries put that word under the same root as haya', today's word, and as hayat, life. Some classical scholars, Ibn al-Qayyim among them, drew the connection: haya' keeps a heart alive. Then there's a detail in the verse itself. The Qur'an describes her modesty by the way she walks. Not her clothes; the verse doesn't mention them. Her pace, her bearing. And in the same verse she speaks, clearly and directly, to a stranger: my father invites you, to pay you for watering for us. Modesty here isn't silence or shrinking. It's a way of carrying yourself that's dignified and unhurried, while still saying exactly what needs saying. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says haya' is a branch of faith. Another, in Bukhari, says haya' brings nothing but good. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself was described by a companion as shyer than a young woman behind her curtain, so haya' in Islam was never only for women. This week has been full of people who carry themselves well. The poets who remember. A king who smiled at an ant. A bird who knew. A queen who thought it through. Al-mudtarr. A heart held steady. And today, a woman whose modesty is a walk.
screen: `I AM NEEDY OF WHATEVER GOOD.` · `SHE CAME WALKING SHYLY.` · `HAYA' AND HAYAT: MODESTY AND LIFE.` · `A WALK, AND A CLEAR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry yourself gently. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice your posture right now. Shoulders, jaw, hands. Then picture walking into the next room you'll enter today, a kitchen, an office, a classroom. Picture walking in without rushing, without performing, without shrinking either. Just at an even pace, with your head level. Picture saying what you need to say simply, and stopping. If you pray, you can repeat Musa's words from the shade: my Lord, I need whatever good You send me. The bell holds the time.
Haya'. Modesty, shyness, a sense of dignity before God and people; in the hadith, a branch of faith that brings nothing but good. Today's word.
Your line: modesty is a walk. Today, walk into one room more slowly than usual, and say one thing plainly. Day five hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of haya' as a quality of character for both men and women, shown in speech, bearing and conduct, and many recite Musa's prayer from 28:24 in times of need.

original.note: Arabic: haya', modesty, from the same root as hayat, life.

trapdoor: what you thought: modesty means covering up and keeping quiet.
what it means: a dignified way of carrying yourself, unhurried and unshowy, that still speaks clearly.
what a scholar hears: 'ala istihya', from h-y-y, the root of hayat; and the hadith that haya' is a branch of faith (Bukhari 9, Muslim 35) and brings only good (Bukhari 6117).

notes: Week-end day (519–525): the teach names the week's lines.
Pickthall 28:24 and 28:25 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording.
Haya' and hayat from the same root (h-y-y): standard lexical point; the link 'haya' keeps the heart alive' is attributed to classical scholars generally (e.g. Ibn al-Qayyim); confirm.
Hadith numbers (Bukhari 9, 6117, 3562; Muslim 35) cited from memory; confirm. The companion describing the Prophet's shyness is Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.
28:25's 'one of the two women' is unnamed in the Qur'an; the script leaves her unnamed.
